<!-- slide 3 -->
## Anscombe's Quartet {.smaller}

[Why we visualize]{.eyebrow}

### Same statistics, different shapes

Four datasets with identical means, variance, correlation (0.816), and regression line. Summary statistics alone can hide the shape of your data, so plot first.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: "78%"
#| fig-align: center

RED_LINE = "#D73A2B"   # one-off, sampled from reference (not theme palette)
GOLD_PT  = "#DB9716"

anscombe = load_anscombe()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7, 4.6),
                         sharex=True, sharey=True, constrained_layout=True)
for ax, (dataset, g) in zip(axes.flat, anscombe.groupby("dataset")):
    m, b = np.polyfit(g["x"], g["y"], 1)
    xs = np.linspace(2, 20, 50)
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED_LINE, lw=1.8, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter(g["x"], g["y"], color=GOLD_PT, s=55, alpha=0.9,
               edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.6, zorder=3)
    ax.set_title(f"Dataset {dataset}", loc="left", fontsize=10)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.supxlabel("x"); fig.supylabel("y")
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python
RED_LINE = "#D73A2B"   # regression line
GOLD_PT  = "#DB9716"   # data points

anscombe = load_anscombe()

# CREATE one shared 2x2 canvas; sharex/sharey so panels line up
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7, 4.6),
                         sharex=True, sharey=True,
                         constrained_layout=True)

for ax, (dataset, g) in zip(axes.flat, anscombe.groupby("dataset")):
    m, b = np.polyfit(g["x"], g["y"], 1)          # the identical fit
    xs = np.linspace(2, 20, 50)
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED_LINE, lw=1.8)            # CALL: line
    ax.scatter(g["x"], g["y"], color=GOLD_PT, s=55, alpha=0.9, # CALL: points
               edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.6)
    ax.set_title(f"Dataset {dataset}", loc="left", fontsize=10)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.supxlabel("x"); fig.supylabel("y")
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.58em; color: #666666; text-align: center;"}
Source: Anscombe (1973), *The American Statistician* 27(1), 17–21.
:::

<!-- slide 4 -->
## The Datasaurus Dozen {.smaller}

[Why we visualize]{.eyebrow}

### Identical stats, different shapes

All 13 datasets share almost the same summary statistics: x̄ ≈ 54.3, ȳ ≈ 47.8, σx ≈ 16.8, σy ≈ 26.9. Same numbers, wildly different pictures.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7.4
#| fig-dpi: 150
#| out-width: "80%"
#| fig-align: center

DOT = "#5B7C99"   # one-off slate (not theme palette)

dd = load_datasaurus()

order = ["dino", "away", "h_lines", "v_lines", "x_shape",
         "star", "high_lines", "dots", "circle", "bullseye",
         "slant_up", "slant_down", "wide_lines"]

# CREATE 3x5 canvas on the cream page colour
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 5, figsize=(12, 7.4),
                         constrained_layout=True, facecolor=CREAM)

for ax, name in zip(axes.flat, order):
    g = dd[dd["dataset"] == name]
    ax.scatter(g["x"], g["y"], color=DOT, s=14, alpha=0.85, linewidths=0)  # CALL
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    ax.set_facecolor("white")
    ax.set_box_aspect(1)                 # each panel a square tile
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for sp in ax.spines.values():        # thin border per tile
        sp.set_color(LINE); sp.set_linewidth(0.8)

# 13 shapes, 15 cells: hide the two spares (stats now live in the text)
axes.flat[13].set_visible(False)
axes.flat[14].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python
DOT = "#5B7C99"   # one-off slate (not theme palette)

dd = load_datasaurus()

order = ["dino", "away", "h_lines", "v_lines", "x_shape",
         "star", "high_lines", "dots", "circle", "bullseye",
         "slant_up", "slant_down", "wide_lines"]

# CREATE 3x5 canvas; each panel a square tile with a thin border
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 5, figsize=(12, 7.4),
                         constrained_layout=True, facecolor=CREAM)

for ax, name in zip(axes.flat, order):
    g = dd[dd["dataset"] == name]
    ax.scatter(g["x"], g["y"], color=DOT, s=14, alpha=0.85, linewidths=0)  # CALL
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    ax.set_facecolor("white")
    ax.set_box_aspect(1)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_color(LINE); sp.set_linewidth(0.8)

axes.flat[13].set_visible(False)
axes.flat[14].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.58em; color: #666666; text-align: center;"}
Source: Matejka & Fitzmaurice (2017), [Same Stats, Different Graphs](https://www.research.autodesk.com/publications/same-stats-different-graphs/), ACM CHI.
:::

## The Genomics Data Explosion {.smaller}

[Why we visualize]{.eyebrow}

### Scale of the problem

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}

- <span style="color: var(--gv-muted);">**1 to 2 exabytes** of data produced on YouTube per year</span>

- <span style="color: var(--gv-green); font-weight: 700;">220 million genomes</span> sequenced <span style="color: var(--gv-green); font-weight: 700;">per year</span>

- Equivalent to <span style="color: var(--gv-muted); font-weight: 700;">40 exabytes</span> per year

- That's more than <span style="color: var(--gv-green); font-weight: 700;">20 times</span> more than YouTube produces

::: fragment
For years we struggled to collect biological data, but now our biggest bottleneck is [analyzing and interpreting it]{.alt}
